unit.name: Networks and Cyber Security
unit.subtitle: How data moves between computers, the protocols involved and how to keep networks safe

lessons.title: Networks, Network Types and Protocols
lessons.description: PAN, LAN and WAN, wired vs wireless trade-offs, and the protocols that make the internet work.
lessons.content_html:
What Is a Computer Network?

A computer network is two or more devices linked so they can exchange data and share resources. Networks range from two laptops connected at home to millions of devices spanning the globe. Without networks, every device would be an island: no email, no streaming, no online banking, no shared printing in a school.

Networks offer significant advantages: files can be shared between users without physical media, a single internet connection can be shared across many devices, centralised storage makes backups easier, and users can communicate in real time. The disadvantages include the cost of setting up and maintaining the hardware, the risk of spreading malware across connected devices, and the need for security measures to protect shared data.

Key Fact

The three main network types are: PAN (Personal Area Network) — a very short-range network between personal devices, typically using Bluetooth; LAN (Local Area Network) — covers a small area such as a school or office and is usually owned by one organisation; WAN (Wide Area Network) — covers a large geographic area and is typically under collective or distributed ownership.

PAN, LAN and WAN

A PAN (Personal Area Network) connects devices within the range of a single person, typically up to about ten metres. Bluetooth is the technology you need to know for PANs: it connects a smartphone to wireless earbuds, a laptop to a wireless keyboard, or a smartwatch to a phone. PANs are low-cost and require no infrastructure, but they are only suitable for personal device pairing, not for sharing resources across an organisation.

A LAN (Local Area Network) covers a relatively small area — a school, a hospital ward, an office floor. The hardware (cables, switches, routers) is usually owned and managed by the organisation itself. LANs typically offer high-speed connections because devices are physically close together and the network infrastructure is dedicated to that organisation.

A WAN (Wide Area Network) covers a wide geographic area, connecting multiple LANs across cities, countries, or continents. WANs rely on third-party telecommunications infrastructure — leased telephone lines, undersea cables, or satellite links — meaning no single organisation owns the whole network. The internet is the largest example of a WAN.

LANs cover a small area; WANs cover a large area. LANs are typically owned by one organisation; WANs use infrastructure owned by multiple parties. LANs tend to offer higher speeds and lower latency because devices are physically close; WAN speeds vary and depend on the quality of telecommunications links between sites. Setting up a LAN is relatively low-cost; connecting to a WAN typically involves paying for leased lines or internet service provider fees. Both can use wired or wireless technology.

Wired vs Wireless Networks

Wired networks use physical cables. Fibre optic cable carries data as pulses of light and can achieve very high speeds over long distances with minimal signal degradation — it is used for backbone connections between buildings and for connecting homes to the internet. Copper cable (such as twisted-pair Ethernet cable) is cheaper and easier to install, but its speed and range are more limited and it is more susceptible to electrical interference.

Wireless networks transmit data using radio waves. The main advantage is mobility: devices can connect from anywhere within range without needing a physical cable. This makes wireless ideal for laptops, tablets and smartphones. However, wireless connections are generally slower and less reliable than wired equivalents, more susceptible to interference from walls and other devices, and potentially less secure because any device within range can attempt to connect. Wireless signals can also be degraded by distance from the access point.

Network Protocols

A network protocol is an agreed set of rules for communication. Without protocols, devices from different manufacturers using different operating systems could not exchange data reliably. Protocols define how data is formatted, addressed, transmitted, and error-checked.

Key Fact

The protocols you must know: IP (addresses and routes data packets across networks), TCP (sets up the connection and ensures reliable delivery), HTTP (transfers web pages), HTTPS (encrypted web transfer), SMTP (sends emails), IMAP (receives and manages emails on a mail server).

IP (Internet Protocol) — assigns a unique address to every device on the internet and handles the addressing and routing of data packets. When data is sent across the internet, IP ensures each packet is labelled with the source and destination address so routers can forward it along the correct path.

TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) — works with IP to set up a reliable connection between two devices. TCP breaks data into packets, numbers them, and checks that all packets arrive and are reassembled correctly. If a packet is lost, TCP requests it to be sent again.

HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) — defines how web browsers and web servers exchange web pages. When you type a website address, your browser sends an HTTP request; the server responds with the page content.

HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) — an encrypted version of HTTP. The data exchanged between browser and server is scrambled so it cannot be read if intercepted. Essential for banking, shopping and login pages.

SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) — used to send emails from a client to a mail server, and between mail servers. When you press Send, your email application uses SMTP.

IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol) — allows an email client to access and manage email stored on a remote mail server. Emails remain on the server and are synchronised across all devices. This is important: note that POP3 is not on the required protocol list for this specification — IMAP is the email-receiving protocol to know.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions asking you to ‘describe’ or ‘compare’ network types, always anchor your answer to the key distinguishing features: geographic scale, ownership, and typical speed/reliability. Do not confuse PAN with LAN — a PAN connects personal devices over a very short range (Bluetooth); a LAN connects many devices across a building. For protocol questions, know the purpose of each protocol (not just its expanded acronym). Note that IMAP is the email-receiving protocol in this specification; do not write POP3.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • PANs connect personal devices over short ranges (Bluetooth); LANs cover a small area with single-organisation ownership; WANs span wide geographic areas with distributed ownership — the internet is the largest WAN.
  • Wired connections (fibre and copper) offer higher speed and reliability; wireless offers mobility but is slower, less secure, and more prone to interference.
  • Protocols are agreed rules for data communication. Key protocols: IP (addressing/routing), TCP (reliable delivery), HTTP/HTTPS (web), SMTP (sending email), IMAP (receiving email).

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a Local Area Network (LAN)?
A) A network that connects personal devices such as a phone and wireless earbuds
B) A network covering a wide geographic area under distributed ownership
C) A network covering a small area such as a school building, owned by one organisation
D) A network that uses Bluetooth to connect devices within a few metres
practice_questions.marks: C) A network covering a small area such as a school building, owned by one organisation [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the network type that uses Bluetooth to connect personal devices over a short range.
practice_questions.marks: PAN (Personal Area Network) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State one advantage and one disadvantage of using a wireless network instead of a wired network.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Advantage — mobility/no physical cables needed, devices can connect from anywhere in range. Disadvantage — slower/less reliable than wired, more susceptible to interference, or less secure (any device in range may attempt to connect).
Secure: Both advantage and disadvantage correctly identified with brief context.
Developing: One correct point with the other vague or missing.
Emerging: One correct point only. [1 mark per point, 2 marks total]

practice_questions.text: Explain the purpose of the TCP/IP protocols when data is sent across the internet.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains both parts distinctly — IP assigns addresses and routes packets across the network; TCP sets up the connection, breaks data into numbered packets, checks they all arrive, and requests retransmission of lost packets. Connects both to how they work together.
Secure: Both IP and TCP explained with reasonable detail.
Developing: One protocol well explained, the other only briefly mentioned.
Emerging: Vague description of data being sent across the internet with little accurate detail. [2 marks per protocol]

practice_questions.text: Compare a LAN and a WAN. In your answer, refer to geographic scale, ownership and typical connection speed.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Structured comparison covering all three areas: (1) LAN covers a small area (e.g. a school); WAN covers a wide geographic area (e.g. the internet). (2) LAN hardware is owned by one organisation; WAN relies on infrastructure owned by multiple parties. (3) LANs typically offer faster, more reliable connections as devices are physically close; WAN speeds vary and depend on leased telecommunications links.
Secure: Covers two of three areas with accurate comparison.
Developing: Some accurate points but comparison structure weak; may describe each network separately rather than compare.
Emerging: Basic identification of differences with little development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between HTTP and HTTPS, and state when HTTPS should be used.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: HTTP transfers web pages without encryption, so data could be intercepted. HTTPS adds encryption so data exchanged between browser and server cannot be read if intercepted. Should be used whenever sensitive data is sent, e.g. banking, shopping, login pages. Links to security benefit.
Secure: Correct difference explained; use case identified.
Developing: States HTTPS is more secure without explaining why; or explains why without stating when.
Emerging: Only names the protocols without meaningful explanation. [4 marks]

A very short-range network connecting personal devices. Bluetooth is the technology to know for this network type.
Covers a relatively small geographical area such as a single building or campus. It is usually owned and managed by a single person or organisation.
Covers a wide geographic area and is often under collective or distributed ownership. The internet is the largest WAN in existence.
A set of rules that govern how data is transmitted and received across a network. Both the sender and receiver must follow the same protocol for communication to succeed.

lessons.title: Network Security and the TCP/IP Model
lessons.description: Authentication, encryption, firewalls, MAC filtering and how the four-layer TCP/IP model organises traffic.
lessons.content_html:
Why Network Security Matters

Every device connected to a network is a potential target. A school network holds thousands of student records; a hospital network carries patient data; a retail network processes payment details. Network security refers to the combination of measures used to protect these systems. No single measure is perfect, so effective security uses multiple layers working together.

Key Fact

The four network security methods you must know are: authentication (verifying who a user is), encryption (scrambling data so it cannot be read if intercepted), firewalls (monitoring and filtering network traffic), and MAC address filtering (allowing or blocking devices based on their hardware address).

Authentication

Authentication is the first line of defence. Before a user can access a network, the system must confirm who they are. The simplest form is a username and password: the username identifies the user, and the password proves it is really them. Stronger authentication uses multiple factors — for example, a password combined with a one-time code sent to a mobile phone (two-factor authentication). Authentication ensures that only authorised users can access resources, even if an attacker knows the network exists.

Encryption

Encryption protects data in transit and in storage. When data is encrypted, it is transformed into ciphertext — an unreadable scramble of characters. Only someone with the correct decryption key can restore it to its original form. On networks, encryption is used by HTTPS (which encrypts web traffic between a browser and a server) and by secure email systems. Even if an attacker intercepts encrypted data travelling across a network, they cannot read it without the key.

Firewalls

A firewall acts as a gatekeeper between a trusted internal network and an untrusted external network such as the internet. It examines each packet of data and decides whether to allow it through or block it, based on predefined rules. For example, a school might configure its firewall to block traffic to certain categories of website, or to block all incoming connections on ports not needed for school systems. Firewalls can be hardware devices, software running on a computer, or a combination of both.

MAC Address Filtering

Every network interface card (NIC) has a unique MAC address (Media Access Control address) assigned by its manufacturer. MAC address filtering uses this address to control which devices can connect to a network. A network administrator creates a list of approved MAC addresses; only devices on the list can access the network. This is useful for restricting access to a wireless network in a school, preventing unauthorised devices from connecting even if they know the Wi-Fi password. A limitation is that MAC addresses can be changed in software (called MAC spoofing), so it should not be relied upon as the sole security measure.

A well-secured network layers its defences. Authentication prevents unauthorised users from logging in. MAC address filtering prevents unauthorised devices from connecting. A firewall blocks suspicious traffic that does reach the network. Encryption protects data even if it is intercepted in transit. Each layer compensates for the weaknesses of the others. For example, a firewall cannot protect against an attacker who already has valid credentials — but authentication can. Together, they provide a much stronger defence than any single measure alone.

The Four-Layer TCP/IP Model

When data travels across a network, the process is organised into four distinct layers. Each layer handles a specific job, and data passes through all four layers on its way from sender to receiver. This is the TCP/IP model, named after its two key protocols. Using layers means each component can be developed and updated independently: a new application protocol can be added without changing how packets are routed.

Key Fact

The four layers of the TCP/IP model, from top to bottom: Application (where network applications operate — HTTP, HTTPS, SMTP, IMAP), Transport (sets up communication and manages packets — TCP), Internet (addressing and routing packets — IP), Link (network hardware and drivers — NIC, OS device drivers).

Application layer — this is where network applications operate. Web browsers, email clients, and file transfer tools all sit at this layer. The protocols at this layer — HTTP, HTTPS, SMTP, and IMAP — define how those applications format and exchange data.

Transport layer — sets up the communication session between two hosts and agrees settings such as the size of data packets. TCP operates at this layer, providing reliable, ordered delivery by breaking data into packets, numbering them, and checking they all arrive correctly. If a packet is lost, TCP requests it again.

Internet layer — handles addressing and routing. IP operates at this layer: it assigns a source and destination IP address to each packet and determines the best path through the network of routers to reach the destination.

Link layer — the lowest layer, responsible for the physical transmission of data across a single link. The network interface card (NIC) sits here, along with the operating system’s device drivers that communicate with it. This layer handles the actual electrical or optical signals on the cable or wireless channel.

When data is sent, it passes down through the layers on the sender’s device (Application → Transport → Internet → Link), crosses the network physically, and then passes up through the layers on the receiver’s device (Link → Internet → Transport → Application) to be reassembled and delivered to the application.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For TCP/IP model questions, learn which protocols sit at which layer and the function of each layer. The most common mistakes are: placing IP at the Transport layer (it belongs at the Internet layer), or placing TCP at the Application layer (it belongs at Transport). Remember: HTTP, HTTPS, SMTP and IMAP are all at the Application layer; TCP is at Transport; IP is at Internet; and the NIC and OS drivers are at the Link layer. When explaining network security measures, link each method to what it protects against — do not just define the term.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The four network security methods are: authentication (verifying identity), encryption (protecting data in transit), firewalls (filtering traffic by rules), and MAC address filtering (allowing only approved hardware addresses).
  • The TCP/IP model has four layers: Application (where protocols like HTTP, HTTPS, SMTP, IMAP operate), Transport (TCP — reliable packet delivery), Internet (IP — addressing and routing), and Link (NIC and OS drivers).
  • Using multiple security layers is more effective than relying on any single measure, as each compensates for the limitations of the others.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following protocols operates at the Internet layer of the TCP/IP model?
A) HTTP
B) SMTP
C) TCP
D) IP
practice_questions.marks: D) IP [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two protocols that operate at the Application layer of the TCP/IP model.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any two of: HTTP, HTTPS, SMTP, IMAP. [1 mark for two correct answers]

practice_questions.text: State one difference between a firewall and MAC address filtering as network security measures.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A firewall monitors and filters data packets based on rules about the content and source/destination of traffic; MAC address filtering controls which devices can connect to the network based on their hardware address, operating before data is transmitted.
Secure: Correct contrast identifying the different aspect each measure targets.
Developing: Describes one measure accurately, the other vaguely.
Emerging: Names both without meaningful comparison. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what encryption does to data and why it is important for network security.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Encryption converts data into ciphertext using a key so it cannot be read by anyone who intercepts it in transit. Only the holder of the correct decryption key can restore it. This is critical for protecting sensitive data such as passwords, financial details and messages on a network, even if an attacker gains access to the data stream.
Secure: Correct explanation of encryption with a clear security benefit.
Developing: States data is scrambled/unreadable but does not explain the key mechanism or security benefit clearly.
Emerging: Vague description — e.g. 'makes data safe' without explanation. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of each of the four layers of the TCP/IP model. Name at least one protocol or hardware component associated with each layer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: All four layers accurately described with correct protocols/hardware: Application (HTTP, HTTPS, SMTP, IMAP — where applications operate), Transport (TCP — sets up communication, manages packets, ensures delivery), Internet (IP — addressing and routing packets), Link (NIC, OS drivers — physical transmission). Explains the flow of data down through layers on send and up on receive.
Secure: All four layers identified with accurate roles; some protocols/hardware correctly placed.
Developing: Three layers described with mostly correct protocols; one layer confused or missing.
Emerging: Two or fewer layers described; protocols placed at incorrect layers. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text: A school wants to prevent unauthorised devices from connecting to its wireless network. Explain how MAC address filtering works and identify one limitation of this approach.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Every NIC has a unique MAC address assigned by its manufacturer. The network administrator creates a list of approved MAC addresses; only devices on the list are permitted to connect, even if they know the Wi-Fi password. Limitation: MAC addresses can be changed in software (MAC spoofing), allowing an attacker to impersonate an approved device.
Secure: Correct explanation of how filtering works and a valid limitation.
Developing: Explains that only approved devices can connect but does not explain how the filtering is applied; or explains correctly without identifying a limitation.
Emerging: Vague description of blocking devices. [4 marks]

glossary_terms.definition: The processes, practices and technologies designed to protect network infrastructure, devices and data from unauthorised access, damage or attack.
The process of verifying the identity of a user or device before granting access to a network or system.
The process of converting data into a coded form (ciphertext) using a key, so it cannot be read by anyone who does not have the decryption key.
A network security device that monitors incoming and outgoing network traffic and decides whether to allow or block specific traffic based on a defined set of security rules.
A unique hardware address permanently assigned to a network interface card by the manufacturer. It is used to identify devices at the network hardware level.

A four-layer model that describes how data is transmitted across a network. The layers are: Application, Transport, Internet, and Link. Each layer has a specific role in preparing data for transmission.

lessons.title: Cyber Security Threats and Social Engineering
lessons.description: Malware, social engineering tactics, weak passwords and unpatched software, plus penetration testing.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Cyber Security?

Cyber security is the field concerned with defending digital systems and data. It matters to everyone: a UK bank holding millions of customer accounts, a school storing pupil data, a teenager with a social media profile. Cyber threats do not require physical proximity — an attacker can target a system from anywhere in the world, which is what makes them so difficult to defend against.

Threats come from multiple directions. Some exploit technical weaknesses in software or networks. Others exploit the most unpredictable component of any system: the people using it. Understanding how attacks work is the first step towards defending against them.

Social Engineering

Social engineering targets human psychology rather than technical flaws. Attackers create believable scenarios to trick people into doing something they would not normally do — revealing a password, clicking a link, or unlocking a door. The three forms you need to know are blagging, phishing, and shouldering.

Key Fact

The three social engineering techniques: blagging (pretexting) — creating a fabricated scenario to trick a victim into revealing information; phishing — using fraudulent emails or messages to obtain private information; shouldering — observing someone’s private information over their shoulder, such as watching a PIN being entered at a cashpoint.

Blagging (pretexting) involves inventing a convincing story. An attacker might call a company helpdesk pretending to be an IT contractor who urgently needs a user’s login reset, or claim to be a bank employee asking a customer to “verify” their account details. The invented scenario is designed to create a sense of urgency or authority that overrides the target’s normal caution.

Phishing typically arrives as an email or text message that appears to come from a trusted source — a bank, a delivery company, or a well-known retailer. The message creates urgency (“Your account will be suspended”) and directs the target to a fake website designed to harvest their login credentials. Spear phishing is a targeted form aimed at a specific individual, making the deception more convincing.

Shouldering (shoulder surfing) is the simplest form of social engineering: physically watching someone enter private information. It happens at cashpoints, on public transport when someone reads emails over a stranger’s shoulder, or in an office when someone watches a colleague type a password.

Malware

Malware (malicious software) covers a range of programs designed to cause harm. The three types specified for this course are: computer viruses, trojans, and spyware.

A computer virus attaches itself to an existing file or program. When the infected file is opened or shared, the virus copies itself to other files. Viruses require a host file and rely on user action to spread — for example, opening an infected email attachment or copying a file from an infected USB drive.

A trojan (sometimes called a trojan horse) disguises itself as useful software — a free game, a codec, an update. Once installed, it operates silently in the background. Unlike a virus, a trojan does not self-replicate; instead, it typically opens a back door that allows an attacker to access the infected system remotely.

Spyware runs hidden in the background and monitors the user’s activity. A keylogger is a common form: it records every key pressed, capturing passwords, bank details, and messages. The data is transmitted back to the attacker without the user knowing the software is even present.

Other Threats

Pharming redirects users to a fake website without them clicking any suspicious link. Unlike phishing (which relies on deceiving the user into clicking), pharming tampers with the underlying address resolution process — so even typing a correct bank web address into a browser might lead to a fake copy of that site.

Several other conditions create vulnerabilities. Weak and default passwords are easily guessed or cracked: using “password”, “admin”, or a device’s factory-set password leaves an obvious entry point. Misconfigured access rights occur when users have more permissions than their role requires — for example, a data entry clerk with admin rights could accidentally or deliberately delete critical records. Removable media (USB drives, external disks) can introduce malware when plugged into a device, either deliberately or because the drive was infected elsewhere. Unpatched or outdated software contains known security vulnerabilities that developers have since fixed in updates — systems running old software are exposed to attacks that exploit those known weaknesses.

Penetration Testing

Penetration testing is a defensive technique: organisations hire specialist testers to attack their own systems legally and intentionally. The goal is to discover weaknesses before a malicious attacker does. There are two key approaches:

Key Fact

Two types of penetration test: internal (white-box) — the tester has knowledge of the system and possibly basic credentials, simulating a malicious insider such as a rogue employee; external (black-box) — the tester has no knowledge of the system or credentials, simulating an outside attacker with no prior access.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For ‘define’ questions on social engineering terms, precision matters. Blagging involves creating an invented scenario (not just lying — there must be a fabricated backstory). Shouldering means physically observing private information — it is not a digital attack. In malware questions, remember the scope: for this specification, the malware types are virus, trojan and spyware. Worms and ransomware are not in the required list — do not bring them in. For penetration testing, always distinguish which type simulates an insider threat (internal) and which simulates an external attacker.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Social engineering exploits people rather than technology: blagging uses a fake scenario, phishing uses fraudulent messages, and shouldering means physically watching someone enter private data.
  • Malware types to know: viruses (attach to files and spread), trojans (disguised as legitimate software, open back doors), and spyware (secretly monitor and transmit user activity).
  • Penetration testing is a defensive measure: internal testing simulates a rogue insider; external testing simulates an outside attacker. Both find vulnerabilities before real attackers do.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes pharming?
A) Sending fraudulent emails to trick users into revealing their passwords
B) Physically watching someone enter a PIN at a cashpoint
C) Redirecting users from a legitimate website to a fraudulent one without them clicking a malicious link
D) Using a fabricated scenario to trick someone into revealing information over the phone
practice_questions.marks: C) Redirecting users from a legitimate website to a fraudulent one without them clicking a malicious link [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two types of malware that are covered in this topic.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any two of: computer virus / trojan / spyware. [1 mark for two correct answers]

practice_questions.text: State the difference between blagging and phishing as forms of social engineering.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Blagging involves creating a fabricated scenario (pretext) — typically in a phone call or face-to-face interaction — to manipulate someone into revealing information. Phishing uses fraudulent emails or messages to trick users into visiting a fake site or providing credentials.

Developing: Vague distinction — e.g. one involves emails, the other phone calls — without explaining the mechanism.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a computer virus spreads and describe one way an organisation could protect itself from virus infections.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A virus attaches itself to a legitimate file; when the file is opened or shared (e.g. as an email attachment or via a USB drive), the virus copies itself to other files or systems. Protection: keeping anti-malware software up to date so it detects known virus signatures; or disabling autorun on removable media to prevent viruses spreading automatically.
Secure: Spread correctly explained; protection method valid and linked to the mechanism.
Developing: Spread described vaguely or protection described without link to virus behaviour.
Emerging: Identifies viruses as harmful without explaining spread. [2 marks per part]

practice_questions.text: Explain what penetration testing is and describe the difference between internal and external penetration testing.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Penetration testing is the authorised process of attempting to access a system without normal credentials to find and fix vulnerabilities. Internal testing: the tester has some knowledge or credentials, simulating a malicious insider. External testing: the tester has no knowledge or credentials, simulating an outside attacker. Both types aim to identify weaknesses before real attackers exploit them.
Secure: Correct definition and both types distinguished with the key credential/knowledge difference.
Developing: Correct definition; types partially distinguished.
Emerging: Describes penetration testing vaguely; does not distinguish between types. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: A company discovers that many staff are using weak passwords and running unpatched software. Explain why each of these poses a security risk and suggest one measure for each to reduce the risk.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Weak passwords — easily guessed or cracked by automated tools; risk is unauthorised access. Measure: enforce a password policy (minimum length, mixed characters) or use multi-factor authentication. Unpatched software — known vulnerabilities are publicly documented; attackers write exploits targeting them. Measure: configure automatic updates or establish a regular patching schedule. Both risks connected to real consequences (data breach, service disruption). Measures evaluated for effectiveness.
Secure: Both risks accurately explained with appropriate measures.
Developing: Both risks identified; measures partially correct or not linked to the specific risk.
Emerging: One risk explained; measure vague or missing. [8 marks]

glossary_terms.definition: The processes, practices and technologies designed to protect networks, computers, programs and data from attack, damage or unauthorised access.
The art of manipulating people into giving up confidential information or taking actions that compromise security, by exploiting trust rather than technical vulnerabilities.
A social engineering technique in which an attacker creates a fabricated scenario (a pretext) to engage a target and manipulate them into revealing information or performing an action.
A social engineering attack that uses fraudulent emails, text messages or fake websites to trick users into revealing passwords, bank details or other private information.
Observing a person's private information over their shoulder, for example watching someone enter a PIN at a cashpoint or reading their password as they type it.
An umbrella term for any software that is hostile, intrusive or designed to damage, disrupt or gain unauthorised access to a computer system.
A type of malware that attaches itself to legitimate files and spreads by copying itself to other files or systems when those files are opened or shared.
Malware disguised as legitimate software. Once installed, a trojan can give an attacker remote access or install other malware, without the user being aware.
Malware that secretly monitors and records a user's activity — such as keystrokes and websites visited — and transmits this information to an attacker without the user's knowledge.
A cyber attack that redirects a user from a legitimate website to a fraudulent one, typically by corrupting DNS entries or modifying local hosts files, without the user clicking a malicious link.
The authorised process of attempting to gain access to a system's resources without normal credentials, in order to identify and fix security vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them.

lessons.title: Detecting and Preventing Cyber Threats
lessons.description: Biometrics, password systems, CAPTCHA, email confirmation and automatic updates as defences.
lessons.content_html:
Defence in Depth

No single security measure can stop every attack. The most effective approach is layered defence: stacking multiple measures so that if one fails, another is still in place. This lesson covers the five specific prevention measures from the specification: biometric measures, password systems, CAPTCHA, email confirmation, and automatic software updates. Understanding what each one does — and crucially, what it is protecting against — is more useful than simply memorising definitions.

Key Fact

The five security measures to know: biometric measures (authenticating by physical characteristics), password systems (verifying identity by secret credentials), CAPTCHA (distinguishing humans from automated bots), email confirmation (verifying a user’s identity or an action via their email account), and automatic software updates (patching known vulnerabilities as soon as fixes are available).

Biometric Measures

Biometric measures authenticate users using unique physical characteristics. Common examples include fingerprint scanning, facial recognition, and iris scanning. These are particularly common on mobile devices: a smartphone’s fingerprint sensor or face unlock feature uses biometric data stored securely on the device to confirm that the person picking up the phone is its owner.

Biometrics offer a significant advantage over passwords: a fingerprint cannot be forgotten and is very difficult for another person to replicate. However, biometric data is permanent — unlike a password, you cannot change your fingerprints if they are ever compromised. This is why biometric data is usually combined with another factor rather than used alone.

Password Systems

A password system is the most widely used form of authentication. A strong password is long, contains a mix of letters, numbers and symbols, and is not based on easily guessed information such as a name or date of birth. Weak or default passwords are a major vulnerability: attackers use automated tools to systematically try common passwords (a dictionary attack) or all possible combinations (a brute-force attack).

Password systems become significantly stronger when combined with a second factor. Two-factor authentication (2FA) requires the user to provide something they know (the password) and something they have (such as a one-time code sent to their phone). Even if an attacker obtains the password, they cannot log in without also having access to the second factor.

Length matters more than complexity. A short, complex password like X7!q is cracked far faster by brute force than a long passphrase like PurpleElephantRunsFast, because the number of possible combinations grows exponentially with each additional character. A strong password should be at least 12 characters long, mix upper and lower case with numbers and symbols, not be a dictionary word or a predictable modification of one, and be unique to each account (reusing passwords means that if one site is breached, all accounts sharing that password are at risk).

CAPTCHA

CAPTCHA stands for Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart. It is the tick-box, image-selection, or distorted-text puzzle you encounter when logging in or creating an account online. Its purpose is to block automated bots from performing actions at scale — such as creating thousands of fake accounts, submitting spam through a contact form, or attempting to brute-force a login by trying thousands of password combinations rapidly.

CAPTCHA exploits the fact that certain tasks which are trivial for a human brain (identifying traffic lights in a photograph, reading slightly skewed letters) are computationally difficult for automated programs. By requiring users to complete these challenges, websites ensure that an actual human is behind the keyboard. Modern versions use behavioural analysis to assess whether a user interacts with a page in a human-like way, making them more seamless for genuine users while still blocking bots.

Email Confirmation

Email confirmation uses a person’s email account as a secondary verification channel. When a user creates a new account, the site sends a confirmation link to their email address; the account is only activated when the link is clicked. This proves the person registering actually has access to that email address — a bot or an attacker using a fake email address will not be able to complete the confirmation step.

Email confirmation is also used when security-sensitive actions are requested: resetting a password, changing an email address, or authorising a large bank transfer. Sending a one-time link or code to the registered email means an attacker who only knows a password cannot complete the action without also having access to the email inbox.

Key Fact

Biometrics work best on personal devices where a physical characteristic is available. Passwords are universal but weakest when short or reused. CAPTCHA stops automated bot attacks. Email confirmation proves both ownership of an email address and intent to perform an action. Automatic updates close known software vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them. Used together, these measures create a much harder target.

Automatic Software Updates

Automatic software updates address one of the most exploited vulnerabilities in any system: outdated software. Software contains flaws — bugs in its code that, when discovered by attackers, can be exploited to gain unauthorised access, install malware, or crash a system. When a vulnerability is found, developers release a patch (a targeted fix). Unpatched software is exposed to attacks specifically designed to target that known flaw.

Enabling automatic updates means patches are applied as soon as they become available, minimising the window of vulnerability. Manually updating systems is unreliable — users often delay or ignore update prompts. Automatic updates are particularly important for operating systems and security software such as anti-malware tools, which need to know about the latest threats to protect against them.

Consider a banking app on a smartphone. To protect the account, the bank applies several layers: the phone uses biometrics (face or fingerprint) to prevent strangers using the device; a strong password or PIN is required to log in; a CAPTCHA stops automated login attempts; when logging in from a new device, an email confirmation is sent; and the app updates automatically to patch security vulnerabilities. An attacker who defeats one layer still faces the others. Removing any single layer increases risk — but no single layer is the whole defence.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on this topic often ask you to ‘explain’ a measure and link it to a specific threat. Practice saying: “[measure] works by [mechanism], which prevents [threat]”. For example: “CAPTCHA works by presenting challenges that are easy for humans but hard for automated programs, which prevents bots from making large numbers of automated login attempts.” Avoid vague answers like “it makes the system more secure” — always link the mechanism to the specific attack it blocks. In questions asking you to evaluate, mention both strengths and a limitation where possible.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The five prevention measures are: biometrics (unique physical characteristics for authentication, especially on mobile devices), password systems (secret credentials, stronger with 2FA), CAPTCHA (blocking automated bots), email confirmation (verifying identity or intent via a secondary channel), and automatic updates (patching vulnerabilities as fixes become available).
  • Each measure targets a different type of attack; no single measure is sufficient on its own. Layered defence means multiple measures work together to compensate for each other’s limitations.
  • Unpatched software is one of the most exploited vulnerabilities — automatic updates minimise the time between a patch being released and it being installed.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes what a CAPTCHA does?
A) Encrypts data as it travels across a network
B) Filters network traffic based on predefined rules
C) Distinguishes human users from automated programs (bots)
D) Stores a user's fingerprint to unlock a device
practice_questions.marks: C) Distinguishes human users from automated programs (bots) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Give one reason why automatic software updates are important for cyber security.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of: they apply security patches as soon as fixes become available; they reduce the time window during which known vulnerabilities can be exploited; they ensure protection without relying on users to update manually. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State one advantage and one disadvantage of using biometric measures to secure a mobile device.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Advantage — biometric data (e.g. fingerprint) is unique to the individual and cannot be forgotten. Disadvantage — if biometric data is compromised, it cannot be changed like a password can.
Secure: Both points correct with brief context.
Developing: One correct point; the other vague.
Emerging: Names biometrics without addressing the question. [1 mark per point]

practice_questions.text: Explain how email confirmation is used to verify a user's identity and describe one attack it helps prevent.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: When a user registers or requests a sensitive action, the system sends a one-time link or code to their registered email. The user must click the link or enter the code to confirm they have access to that account. This verifies identity beyond just knowing a username. It prevents an attacker who has stolen a password from completing the action without also controlling the victim's email inbox.
Secure: Mechanism correctly explained; attack or risk identified.
Developing: Describes that a link is sent but does not explain what it verifies or what it protects against.
Emerging: Vague description of receiving an email. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why using a long, unique password for each account is more secure than using a short, complex password that is reused across multiple sites.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A longer password increases the number of possible combinations exponentially, making brute-force attacks impractical. A short password (even with symbols) has far fewer combinations and can be cracked quickly. Reusing a password across sites means a single breach of any one site exposes all accounts using that password — attackers test stolen credentials across many services (credential stuffing). A unique password per account limits the blast radius of any single breach.
Secure: Length advantage explained; reuse risk explained with credential stuffing mentioned or implied.
Developing: States that long passwords are harder to crack and reuse is bad, without explaining the mechanism.
Emerging: Only one point made. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: A new social media platform wants to prevent automated bots from creating fake accounts and performing spam actions. Explain, with reference to at least two security measures, how the platform could defend against this.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: CAPTCHA blocks bots from completing account creation forms by presenting challenges easy for humans but hard for automated programs. Email confirmation requires a link to be clicked in a real inbox, preventing fake or disposable emails from activating accounts. Password strength requirements reduce the chance of accounts being compromised by brute force. Evaluates how measures work together — e.g. CAPTCHA stops mass creation; email confirmation stops bots that bypass CAPTCHA; automatic updates ensure the platform itself is not exploited.
Secure: Two or more measures accurately described with links to the specific bot/spam threat.
Developing: Two measures named but mechanisms not clearly linked to the threat.
Emerging: One measure described vaguely. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which security measure uses a person's fingerprint or face to verify their identity, particularly on mobile devices?
A website presents users with a challenge asking them to select all images containing traffic lights before they can log in. Which security measure is this?
Automatic software updates reduce risk by applying _____ as soon as they are available, closing known vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them.
Email confirmation verifies that a user has access to their _____ address, preventing attackers from completing sensitive actions using only a stolen password.
Match each security measure to what it primarily defends against:
right: Automated bots making large numbers of attempts or fake accounts
Attackers completing sensitive actions using a stolen password without email access
Exploitation of known software vulnerabilities on unpatched systems

glossary_terms.definition: Authentication methods that use a person's unique physical characteristics — such as fingerprints, facial structure or iris patterns — to verify their identity.
An authentication system that requires a user to enter a secret sequence of characters that only they should know, in order to gain access to a system or account.

A challenge-response test used on websites and apps to determine whether the user is a human or an automated program (bot). Common forms include selecting images, solving distorted text, or completing simple tasks that are easy for humans but hard for computers.
A security measure in which a system sends a message to a user's registered email address to verify their identity or confirm that they intended to take a particular action.
A feature in which software checks for and installs security patches and updates without requiring manual intervention, ensuring known vulnerabilities are fixed as soon as a fix is available.
